author: Dante
title: Three voices in Hell
about: Dante tells the poem as his own journey. Lost in a dark wood halfway through his life, he is led down through Hell by the shade of the Roman poet Virgil. At the entrance he reads the writing over the gate. In the second circle Francesca, killed with her lover by her husband, tells him that love led them to one death. Far lower, the Greek hero Ulysses, speaking from inside a flame, tells how a short speech sent his old crew on a last voyage.

view.says: Auden cited the writing over Hell’s gate when he explained the wrath of God. That phrase, he wrote, describes no mood in God. It tells what God is like to a person if he twists or denies his tie to God. So Dante, he said, wrote over Hell that Power, Wisdom and Love made it. He added, crediting Landor, that the people of the *Inferno* have no wish to leave.
view.quote: the way in which I experience God if I distort or deny my relation to him
view.source: Introduction to *The Living Thoughts of Kierkegaard* (1952), reprinted as “Søren Kierkegaard” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 176

plates.heading: The writing over the gate: lines 1 to 12
plates.label: Dante

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.why: The chain of rhyme hands each middle sound on: here it rhymes pain, maker and love, and the rhyme the gate leaves open is completed after it; to an Italian, Auden wrote, parting Dante’s matter from this form is unthinkable.
lenses.caption: Letters mark the rhymes. In each group of three the first and third lines rhyme, and the middle one sets the rhyme of the next. Dante devised this chain, terza rima, for the poem and built it on the number three, which his prose ties to the Trinity. To an Italian, Auden wrote, parting what Dante says from this form is unthinkable. Here the second rhyme joins dolore, pain, fattore, maker, and amore, love: what the gate leads to, and who made it. The chain keeps every group open to the next: when the writing ends, duro, I last, has no rhyme yet, and the next three supply oscuro, dark, and duro again.
lenses.stands: The rhyme letters marked on the passage, and what its lines say; its last open sound, at *porta*, returns in [the next three lines](#/read/dante-italian/inf-03:4). The *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *terzina*: Dante devised the chain, built it on three, and kept each group open to the next; it quotes his *Vita Nuova* on three and the Trinity. Baum, *Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4. Auden: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 324.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: anaphora
lenses.plain: the same words at the head of line after line
lenses.why: The threefold opening belongs to the poem’s grave style of pronouncement and says three times where the way leads.
lenses.caption: Three lines begin with the same words, Per me si va: through me is the way. Beginning line after line alike is called anaphora, and it belongs to the poem’s grave style of pronouncement. Each line changes only where the way leads: into the sorrowing city, into eternal pain, among the lost people. The me is a gate. Medieval city gates carried verse inscriptions, and this writing is made in their likeness. In the writing only the ninth line turns to anyone: voi ch’intrate, you who enter.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage and what its lines say; the English of the opening words is Carlyle’s prose. Anaphora as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it; the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *anafora* gives this opening as its example of the poem’s grave style. The verses over city gates: the notes of Bosco and Reggio and of Chiavacci Leonardi on these lines, at the Dartmouth Dante Project.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: In his own prose Dante assigns power, wisdom and love to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
The third *eternal* of the nine lines. Here the word works as an adverb: I last forever.
From Latin *durare*, to make hard, to hold out, to last. That verb comes from *durus*, hard.
Five lines on, Virgil uses the same verb: here all distrust must be left.
Most readers take it as black letters. Others take it as dark, threatening words.
Hard to understand, or hard to bear: readers have long been divided. In the Latin Gospel many of the disciples call a teaching of Christ *durus*, hard.

lenses.why: The gate names its maker by the established attributes of the Trinity, in the lines Auden quoted to explain the wrath of God; and the traveler then uses the gate’s own word, duro, in a second sense.
lenses.caption: The fifth and sixth lines name the gate’s maker as the three persons of God, each by its established attribute: podestate, power, the Father; sapïenza, wisdom, the Son; primo amore, first love, the Spirit. Auden quoted them to explain the wrath of God: what God is like to a person if he twists or denies his tie to God. On the gate duro is a verb, I last, from the Latin for hard. Four lines later the traveler calls the writing’s sense duro, hard. The two rhyme. A rhyme of one form in two senses sets them against each other: the gate lasts, and its meaning is hard to him.
lenses.stands: The words marked on the passage and what its lines say. The attributes of the Trinity: the notes of Singleton, of Bosco and Reggio and of Chiavacci Leonardi on lines 5 and 6. The two senses of *duro*, and a rhyme of one form in two senses: the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *durare*, *duro* and *rima*; Lewis and Short under *duro*. Auden: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 176.

lenses.label: Compare

ties.say: *Dolent* is an archaic English word for sorrowful, from the same Latin root.
*Dole* is an old word for grief, from the same root. In his note Longfellow hears a funeral bell tolling in the two Italian line ends.
Dante’s line begins with the command, *leave*. Longfellow’s begins with what is to be left.

lenses.why: Longfellow gave up rhyme to keep fidelity, as his journal says: each line keeps its place and the chain is lost; Auden wrote that an English Dante, in prose or in Dante’s rhyme, loses something either way.
lenses.caption: Longfellow’s version of 1867 gives each of Dante’s lines one English line, in nearly the same word order. It does not rhyme. In translating Dante, he wrote in his journal, something must be given up, and it must be the rhyme, to keep what he valued more: fidelity. Auden in 1947 weighed an English Dante in prose against one in Dante’s rhyme. English has few rhymes, he wrote, so even the best attempt to keep the form is driven to a falsely poetic choice and order of words. Either way, he said, something is lost. Here the chain is absent, and Dante’s one word duro becomes last and hard.
lenses.stands: The two versions read line against line, and the words tied between them. Longfellow’s reasons are his own: his journal for 7 May 1864 and a letter of 8 May 1867, in Samuel Longfellow’s *Life* of him, vol. 3, pp. 35 and 88, and his note on the first line of the canto. *Dolent* and *dole*: Wiktionary; the Online Etymology Dictionary under *doleful*. Auden: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 324.

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.why: Each sentence names Love first, as the cause, and leaves the lovers as its objects; twice she adds what still holds, and Auden repeated a remark that the people of the Inferno have no wish to leave.
lenses.caption: Francesca makes three sentences on one frame, each with Amor, Love, as its subject. The first two add a law in the present and an act in the past: love seized costui, this man; love seized mi, me. The third is one line: love led noi, us, to one death. One use of such repeating, a handbook of 1593 says, is to put the cause before each effect. In her eight lines here no verb has I or we as subject. Twice she adds what still holds, with ancor, still; the second time it is the love. Explaining the wrath of God, Auden repeated a remark he credited to Landor: the people of the Inferno have no wish to leave.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. In the Italian of her eight lines here eleven verbs take a subject, and none is *I* or *we*. What such repeating does: an English handbook, Henry Peacham’s *The Garden of Eloquence* (1593), under *Epanaphora*; the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *anafora* cites these lines, and Bosco and Reggio’s note names Love as the subject in line 105, the sixth here. Auden: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 176.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: polyptoton
lenses.plain: one root repeated in different forms
lenses.why: Three forms of one root in one line set being loved and loving side by side as near kin, as the law claims; the poem later restates the law with a condition: love kindled by virtue.
lenses.caption: One root comes three times in a single line, each time in a new form: Amor, the noun, love; amato, one who is loved; amar, to love. The figure is called polyptoton. A handbook of 1593 says that words derived from one another please the ear and make the mind consider how near akin the things are. The line is Francesca’s second law: love spares no one who is loved from loving. Later in the poem Virgil says nearly the same with a condition added: love kindled by virtue has always kindled love, once its flame showed (Purgatorio 22, lines 10 to 12).
lenses.stands: The three words marked in the line. Polyptoton as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it; what it does is from an English handbook, Henry Peacham’s *The Garden of Eloquence* (1593), under *Paregmenon*. The sense of the line: the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *perdonare*. Virgil’s words are in [*Purgatorio* 22](#/read/dante-longfellow/pur-22:3), lines 10 to 12; Bosco and Reggio’s note on this line (103 of the canto) sets the two places side by side.

lenses.label: Measure
lenses.meterName: eleven syllables: the last accent always on the tenth, and in these lines another on the sixth

points.say: Stresses meet on the sixth and seventh syllables. The second of them falls on *ratto*, at once.
Seven written syllables count as five: twice a final vowel runs into the vowel that follows.
Here the two vowels stay apart, which is regular after a word like *noi*. The accent on the sixth syllable falls on *noi*, us.

lenses.why: The second and third Amor lines put an accent on every second syllable; the first breaks the run with an accent on the seventh, beside the sixth, a placing that often brings out its word: ratto, at once.
lenses.caption: Dante’s line goes by count: eleven syllables, the last accent always on the tenth. A vowel ending one word usually runs into a vowel beginning the next, and the two count as one syllable. The three lines that begin with Amor, Love, are marked: the rule under each shows the count, and the dots show the voice’s stresses. In the second and third the stresses fall on every second syllable. The first keeps that run to the sixth, then stresses the seventh, right beside it. A stress so placed often brings out its word. The word is ratto, at once: in her first law love takes hold at once.
lenses.stands: The marks drawn on the three lines follow the stresses of the Italian words. The rules of the line are from the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *endecasillabo*, *sinalefe* and *dialefe*: eleven syllables, the tenth accented; vowels that meet run together; a stress set beside a main accent often brings out its word. *Ratto* as *at once*: the same work under *ratto*, which cites this line.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: A phrase of the love poets. Guido Guinizzelli’s song begins with love coming home to the noble heart, and Dante cites that line in his own prose.
Guinizzelli’s verb. In his song the fire of love takes hold in the noble heart.
*Persona* here is the body. The word was a mark of the chivalric and sensual idea of love and beauty.
The verb’s only use in the *Inferno*. The sense is that of sparing a life.
Named for Cain: the first zone of the lowest circle, for those who betrayed their kin. Her husband killed his wife and his own brother. The poem reaches the place in canto 32.
In its proper sense the verb is used of flames. From the image of life as a flame it comes to mean kill.

lenses.why: Francesca states her law in the love poets’ own words, Guinizzelli’s and the young Dante’s; Auden found a warning in her story, and the poem’s later account of love, which he quoted, is that the mind’s love can err.
lenses.caption: Francesca’s first law is the doctrine of the love poets, in their words. Cor gentil, the noble heart, opens Guinizzelli’s song on love, and s’apprende, takes hold, is his verb for love’s fire. An early sonnet of Dante’s says love and the noble heart are one. Auden said in a lecture that Romeo and Juliet do not tell romance from love, and ended by quoting this scene: her story, he said, holds a warning. Elsewhere he quoted the poem’s later account, from Purgatorio 17, as Dante’s view: natural love cannot err, and the mind’s love can. The canto has said that those punished here put reason under desire.
lenses.stands: The glosses: the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under each word; for *piacer* and *Caina*, notes of Singleton, Grandgent and Chiavacci Leonardi. Guinizzelli’s song is on Italian Wikisource; Dante’s sonnet, in the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under its first line. Auden: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, p. 51, from students’ notes; *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 130–31, quoting [*Purgatorio* 17](#/read/dante-longfellow/pur-17:30), lines 94 to 96 (the mind’s love: line 93). Who is punished: [Canto 5](#/read/dante-longfellow/inf-05:12), lines 37 to 39.

plates.heading: Ulysses to his crew: lines 118 to 126
plates.label: Dante

lenses.label: Antithesis
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.why: The antithesis sets two ways to live against each other, a brute’s and the pursuit of virtue and knowledge; Auden heard in this speech the Serpent’s words to Eve, whose promise was knowledge, the speech’s last word.
lenses.caption: The first three lines end the speech Ulysses made to his old crew at the marks Hercules set so that no one should go farther. Its last two lines set two ways of living against each other, hinged on non, not, and ma, but: viver come bruti, to live like brutes, and seguir virtute e canoscenza, to follow virtue and knowledge. An antithesis can make a thing clear by its contrary. Auden, who quoted the same three lines, said that in this speech Ulysses is again the counselor of evil, and that his words are like the Serpent’s to Eve. The Serpent promised Eve knowledge, and canoscenza, knowledge, is the last word of the speech.
lenses.stands: The two phrases marked on the passage. Where the speech is made: [Canto 26](#/read/dante-longfellow/inf-26:35), lines 106 to 109. Antithesis and its use: the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *antitesi*, and *Silva Rhetoricae*. Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 10; the Serpent’s words are Genesis 3:4–5.

lenses.label: Metaphor
lenses.name: metaphor
lenses.plain: one thing spoken of as another
lenses.why: The line turns oars to wings and the voyage to a flight, the poem’s figure for the movement of the soul, and sets folle, mad, inside it: the ship’s speed and a judgment on the voyage in one line.
lenses.caption: One thing is called by the name of another: remi, oars, are made ali, wings, and the voyage is a volo, a flight. Virgil had called the wings of Daedalus an oarage of wings, and Dante turns the phrase around. Elsewhere in the poem wings and flight are a regular figure for the soul’s movement, as in its rising to God. Between the wings and the flight stands folle, mad. So the flight is at once the ship’s swift course and a going astray. Folle is the speaker’s own word, said from inside the flame. For Dante, Auden said, what Ulysses did was at bottom Adam’s original sin.
lenses.stands: The words marked on the passage; the speaking flame is in [Canto 26](#/read/dante-longfellow/inf-26:28), lines 85 to 90. The *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *metafora* discusses this line, and wings and flight as the poem’s figure for the soul; under *folle* it gives the word’s sense, as does the Treccani *Vocabolario*. Virgil’s phrase is *Aeneid* 6.19, with Chiavacci Leonardi’s note on that line (125). Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 10.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: Your seed: the human kind you come from.
From Latin *virtus*, which comes from *vir*, a man: manliness, courage, worth, virtue. Here it has been read as courage.
The base sense is sharp, pointed.
*Orazione* is a term of rhetoric for a set speech, here an exhortation. *Picciola*, little, is his third use of the word in twenty-one lines: his crew, the waking time left to them, his speech.
From Latin *follis*, a bellows or a bag puffed with air, and so an empty head. English *fool* comes from the same Latin word.
They keep bearing to the left, that is, to the south-west.

lenses.why: Virtute, the speech’s word for what men are made to follow, is also the poet’s word, early in the canto, for what must guide his own wit; those lines, Auden wrote, perhaps mean that Dante felt the temptation himself.
lenses.caption: Semenza is seed: the crew are told to consider the stock they come from. Virtute comes from the Latin for manliness, which also meant courage and worth. The word comes once more in the canto, in the poet’s own voice near its start: he reins in his wit so that it does not run where virtue does not guide it. Those lines, Auden wrote, perhaps mean that Dante himself felt the temptation of Ulysses, a lust of curiosity. Ulysses calls his words an orazion, a term of rhetoric for a set speech, and says it made the men so aguti, keen, that he could hardly have held them back.
lenses.stands: The glosses are from the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *semenza*, *virtù*, *acuto*, *orazione* and *mancino*; Lewis and Short under *virtus* and *follis*; the Treccani *Vocabolario* under *folle*. In the Italian of Canto 26 printed here *virtù* or *virtute* comes twice, at [line 22](#/read/dante-italian/inf-26:7) and in the third line here (120). Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 10. What the speech did to the crew is in the lines themselves.

lenses.label: Poem
lenses.what: Where folle, mad, comes in the poem’s hundred cantos (34 of Inferno, 33 of Purgatorio, 33 of Paradiso), and where it is said of a journey

places.said by: the traveler, to Virgil, before he sets out
the devils at the gate of the city of Dis

places.said of: himself, for his bold words to a pope
the foolish, set beside the wise

places.said by: the founder of Monte Cassino, a soul
the traveler, telling what he saw from the stars
places.said of: the crossing (varco) of Ulysses, past Cadiz

lenses.why: The first of the fourteen uses of folle is the traveler’s fear for his own journey and the last his look back at Ulysses’s crossing, so one word marks both journeys.
lenses.caption: In the poem’s hundred cantos folle, mad, comes fourteen times. Four times it is said of a journey. The first of all is the traveler’s: he is not Aeneas and not Paul, he says, and fears his own going may be mad (canto 2). Devils call his road mad (canto 8), and Ulysses says it of his flight (canto 26). The last comes as the traveler tells what he saw from the stars: the mad crossing of Ulysses (canto 94, Paradiso 27). So the poem sets one word on both journeys, first and last in the traveler’s own voice.
lenses.stands: A count of the adjective *folle* (*folle* or *folli*) in the Italian of the whole poem printed here: fourteen places, the same fourteen the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* lists under *folle*. The noun *follia* was left out; who speaks, and of what, was read at each place. The other three journeys: [*Inferno* 2](#/read/dante-italian/inf-02:11), line 35; [*Inferno* 8](#/read/dante-italian/inf-08:30), line 91; [*Paradiso* 27](#/read/dante-italian/par-27:27), lines 82 and 83.

auden.says: In an unfinished book of 1939, Auden said everyone meets a few people he can only feel to be damned, usually intelligent, sensitive and well placed. Hell’s gates, he wrote, stand wide open. The lost may go when they wish; but that would mean admitting there is another life outside, and they fear to, because they would then have to live it. All this they know, and the knowledge is Hell’s flame. Many people, perhaps most, stand with the good pagans of the *Inferno*, desiring without hope; but Limbo, their place, belongs, he said, at the bottom of Purgatory, not at the top of Hell, where Dante’s poem puts it.
auden.source: “The Prolific and the Devourer,” an unfinished book written mostly in 1939; in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), Appendix I, p. 428

auden.says: In 1946 Auden reviewed C. S. Lewis’s *The Great Divorce*. Its teaching aim, he wrote, is to set right a mistaken idea of what Christians hold about Hell and to make plain the words Dante saw over the gate; he quoted the gate’s fourth, fifth and sixth lines in Carlyle’s prose translation. The mistake was to liken God’s law to human law, with an eternal penalty imposed on people without their consent. On doctrine he had two objections, and one touched Dante: whatever Dante did, he said, theology lets no writer show a historical person as a lost soul. Nobody may believe that even of Hitler, still less hope it.
auden.source: “Red Lizards and White Stallions,” *The Saturday Review of Literature*, April 1946; in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 292–95

auden.says: In a talk of January 1943 Auden drew on the canto of the gate. A student of literature in whom nothing happens, he said, finds it out. In a student of physics nothing may happen either, but his skill gets him a good post in industry, so he may live out his life and never learn that he has no passion: that he is one of the trimmers of the *Inferno*, the souls just inside the gate, who earned neither blame nor praise. Auden then gave Virgil’s words about them in the Carlyle and Wicksteed prose of the Modern Library, the edition on his list for the course.
auden.source: “Vocation and Society,” an essay based on a talk of January 1943, in *‘In Solitude, for Company’: W. H. Auden after 1940*, edited by Katherine Bucknell and Nicholas Jenkins (1995), pp. 25–26; also in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), p. 180

auden.says: Auden spoke of Francesca at the end of his New York lecture on *Romeo and Juliet*, given on 6 November 1946 and rebuilt from students’ notes. Romeo and Juliet, he said, do not tell romance from love. He cited Kierkegaard: romantic love can be shown in a single moment, and married love cannot, since a good husband is one every day. Then he said that the tale of Paolo and Francesca holds a warning to be heeded, and gave the scene in the Carlyle and Wicksteed prose, her three sentences on Love included, down to the last words of the canto.
auden.source: Lecture on *Romeo and Juliet*, 6 November 1946, in *Lectures on Shakespeare*, reconstructed and edited by Arthur Kirsch (2000), pp. 51–52

auden.says: Writing on *The Tempest*, Auden said the play shows Nature and Spirit in conflict, lays the fault on Nature and clears Spirit. Dante, he said, holds just the reverse. He quoted three lines of *Purgatorio* 17 in Italian, which say that natural love never errs and that the other love can err by choosing a bad object, or by too little force or too much. In 1941, the year of the course, he had gone to the same canto twice, both times to its lines on love as the seed of all virtue and of each act that earns punishment.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 130–31; the notes to *New Year Letter* (1941); “Eros and Agape,” *The Nation*, 28 June 1941

auden.says: Auden noted that the last voyage of Ulysses seems to be Dante’s invention. Ulysses is damned as a giver of evil counsel. Auden quoted, in Carlyle’s prose, Dante on holding his talent in check, Ulysses on his ardor to know the world, and the close of the speech to the crew. There, he said, Ulysses is again what he was at Troy. He acts like the sea hero of the Romantics, which in Tennyson he becomes. For Dante the deed was worse than blameworthy: at bottom it was Adam’s original sin. Dante’s words on his talent, he added, may mean that Dante felt the same temptation: a lust of curiosity.
auden.quote: the Evil Counsellor whose words echo the words of the Serpent to Eve
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 9–10

auden.says: In 1947 Auden reviewed *The Portable Dante*, whose *Comedy* is Binyon’s translation, in Dante’s rhyme. He judged that version the best so far and set a passage of it beside Longfellow’s and Cary’s, which he counted among the best known. To an Italian, he wrote, parting what Dante says from the form is unthinkable. A reader of English is troubled by the falsely poetic wording and word order that a language poor in rhymes forces on even the best attempt to keep the form. The best English imitation of Dante, he noted, is a passage of Eliot’s in unrhymed three-line groups. Prose or verse, he said, something is lost.
auden.source: “The Essence of Dante,” *The New York Times Book Review*, 29 June 1947; in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 322–25

auden.says: By Donald Pearce’s account, the final examination of the 1941 course was to write out cantos of the *Comedy* from memory, in the Carlyle and Wicksteed prose version. The list began with *Inferno* 3 and 5, the cantos of the first two passages here. Auden asked for seven cantos and came down to five when the class protested. Other witnesses give six.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), p. 153

sources: The text printed here: Dante Alighieri, *La Divina Commedia*, [the Italian](#/read/dante-italian) from Project Gutenberg, no. 1012, and beside it [the translation of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow](#/read/dante-longfellow) (1867), from Project Gutenberg, no. 1004. Auden’s English quotations of the *Inferno* follow [the prose translation of the Temple Classics](#/read/dante-temple) (London: J. M. Dent), whose *Inferno* is John Aitken Carlyle’s. The Modern Library reprinted that translation in 1932, and its volume is the edition named on Auden’s list for the course.

The counts on this page were made on the Italian printed here, among them the adjective *folle* in the whole poem, *virtù* in Canto 26, *ancor* in Canto 5 and the subjects of the verbs in Francesca’s eight lines here.
caveats: What Auden said of Francesca comes from a 1946 lecture rebuilt from students’ notes; he said her story holds a warning and did not say what it is. The remark he credited to Landor has not been found in Landor’s writings, and in 1938 Auden was unsure whose it was.

Six things of Auden’s were read only in extracts from scanned copies: a book of 1939, a note of 1941, a talk of 1943, a lecture of 1946 and two reviews. In 1939 he wrote of Hell’s gates and did not name Dante’s gate.

In the first of Francesca’s lines here the voice may lean harder on *gentil* or on *ratto*; that the meeting stresses bring out *ratto* is this page’s own use of a general rule. In the sixth the subject, read here as Love, is by another reading Paolo.

On the speech of Ulysses the commentaries divide. Some read it as a last piece of false counsel, as Auden did. Others, Bosco and Reggio among them, hear in it what Dante himself held: that to want knowledge is natural to every man.

Under *Poem*, the count of fourteen takes the adjective *folle* alone; the noun *follia* comes twice more in the poem. Auden’s list for the course named an English prose translation; the passages are shown here in Dante’s Italian, with Longfellow’s verse beside it.
